statement.before: An **inference rule** has premises (judgments) above a line and a conclusion below. A set of rules **inductively defines** a relation or predicate: the judgment $J$ holds exactly when it has a **derivation**, a finite tree whose root is $J$, whose every node is the conclusion of a rule instance, and whose children are the premises of that instance (axioms have none). The set is the *least* one closed under the rules; the height of a derivation is a measure for induction on derivations.
statement.after: An **inference rule** has premises (judgments) above a line and a conclusion below. A set of rules with finitely many premises per rule **inductively defines** a relation or predicate: the judgment $J$ holds exactly when it has a **derivation**, a finite tree whose root is $J$, whose every node is the conclusion of a rule instance, and whose children are the premises of that instance (axioms have none). The set is the *least* one closed under the rules; the height of a derivation is a measure for induction on derivations.

idea.before: Argue by well-founded induction on $a$ (this is where termination is used): assume every element below $a$ is confluent. Take $a\to^{*}b$ and $a\to^{*}c$; unless one path is empty, split them as $a\to b_1\to^{*}b$ and $a\to c_1\to^{*}c$. Local confluence at $a$ gives $d_1$ with $b_1\to^{*}d_1\leftarrow^{*}c_1$. Since $b_1$ is below $a$ and confluent, the fork $b\leftarrow^{*}b_1\to^{*}d_1$ closes at some $e$; then $c_1$ (below $a$, confluent) closes $c\leftarrow^{*}c_1\to^{*}d_1\to^{*}e$ at some $f$, and $b\to^{*}e\to^{*}f\leftarrow^{*}c$. Locally confluent checks involve only single steps, so they are finitely many to test, which is why the lemma is useful in practice.
idea.after: Argue by well-founded induction on $a$ (this is where termination is used): assume every element below $a$ is confluent. Take $a\to^{*}b$ and $a\to^{*}c$; unless one path is empty, split them as $a\to b_1\to^{*}b$ and $a\to c_1\to^{*}c$. Local confluence at $a$ gives $d_1$ with $b_1\to^{*}d_1\leftarrow^{*}c_1$. Since $b_1$ is below $a$ and confluent, the fork $b\leftarrow^{*}b_1\to^{*}d_1$ closes at some $e$; then $c_1$ (below $a$, confluent) closes $c\leftarrow^{*}c_1\to^{*}d_1\to^{*}e$ at some $f$, and $b\to^{*}e\to^{*}f\leftarrow^{*}c$. The benefit is that a fork starts with only two single steps; a general relation may nevertheless have infinitely many such forks. Any reduction to finitely many rule-overlap checks needs a separate finite-presentation and coverage argument, not merely this lemma.

idea.before: Induction on the typing derivation, one case per rule, using the canonical forms of 4.2. Constants are values. For $\mathtt{succ}\,t_1$, $\mathtt{pred}\,t_1$ and $\mathtt{iszero}\,t_1$, the induction hypothesis says $t_1$ is a value or steps; if it steps, the congruence rule steps the whole term; if it is a value of type $\mathsf{Nat}$, canonical forms says it is $0$ or $\mathtt{succ}\,nv$, and then a computation rule applies (this is exactly where E-PredZero is needed). For $\mathtt{if}$, a guard that is a value of type $\mathsf{Bool}$ is $\mathtt{true}$ or $\mathtt{false}$, so E-IfTrue or E-IfFalse fires. The converse fails: ill-typed terms like $\mathtt{succ\ true}$ are stuck.
idea.after: Induction on the typing derivation, one case per rule, using the canonical forms of 4.2. Constants are values. For $\mathtt{succ}\,t_1$, $\mathtt{pred}\,t_1$ and $\mathtt{iszero}\,t_1$, the induction hypothesis says $t_1$ is a value or steps; if it steps, the congruence rule steps the whole term; if it is a value of type $\mathsf{Nat}$, canonical forms says it is $0$ or $\mathtt{succ}\,nv$. The outer $\mathtt{succ}$ then is a numeric value; for $\mathtt{pred}$ or $\mathtt{iszero}$ a computation rule applies (in particular E-PredZero is needed). For $\mathtt{if}$, a guard that is a value of type $\mathsf{Bool}$ is $\mathtt{true}$ or $\mathtt{false}$, so E-IfTrue or E-IfFalse fires. The converse fails: $\mathtt{if\ true\ then\ 0\ else\ false}$ is ill typed because its branches have different types, yet it steps to $0$. Being able to step (or already being a value) therefore does not imply typability.
